concepts.def: Formed from alkene monomers joining without loss of atoms; e.g. poly(ethene), poly(propene).
Polymers formed with elimination of a small molecule (usually H₂O or HCl); e.g. polyester, polyamide.
Made by reacting a diol with a dicarboxylic acid; e.g. PET from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.
Made from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid (or diacyl chloride); e.g. nylon-6,6 and Kevlar.
Condensation polymers can be hydrolysed (esters/amides break), but addition polymers are largely non-biodegradable.
Polymers can be recycled, incinerated for energy or used as feedstock for cracking, depending on type.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Polymers & Synthesis — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Polymers & Synthesis brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Polymers & Synthesis.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does the M+ peak in a mass spectrum represent?
options: The molecular ion — formed when a single electron is removed from the whole molecule, giving the relative molecular mass.
Water is bent because oxygen is heavier than hydrogen and weighs the middle down.
The M+ peak shows the mass of the largest fragment after the molecule breaks apart.
The M+ peak shows the mass of a single hydrogen atom added to the molecule.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
options: A strong acid fully dissociates in water; a concentrated acid has a high amount of acid per volume — these are independent properties.
The M+ peak shows the mass of a single hydrogen atom added to the molecule.
Strong and concentrated mean the same thing for acids.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.

mcqs.q: Why does water have a bent shape rather than linear?
options: Water is bent because the hydrogens repel each other and push apart.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
Water is bent because oxygen is heavier than hydrogen and weighs the middle down.
Oxygen has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, giving a tetrahedral electron geometry but a bent molecular shape.
